items.stem: Why prefer a vectorised NumPy operation over a Python for-loop for element-wise maths?

options.text: It runs the computation in optimised compiled code over the whole array
options.rationale: Correct: vectorised ops avoid per-element Python overhead.

options.text: It always uses less memory than a loop
options.rationale: Vectorised ops can use more memory, not less.
The result is the same; only performance differs.

options.text: It is required for arrays larger than 100 elements
options.rationale: There is no such requirement; it is a performance choice.

items.explanation: Correct: vectorised ops avoid per-element Python overhead.

items.stem: Which TWO are good practices for reproducible ML code? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Pin package versions in an environment file
options.rationale: Correct: pinned versions let others recreate the setup.

options.text: Wrap steps in tested functions rather than loose notebook cells
options.rationale: Correct: tested functions reduce hidden-state errors.

options.text: Rely on cells being run in a particular manual order
options.rationale: Hidden execution order causes non-reproducible results.

options.text: Hard-code absolute paths from your own machine
options.rationale: Absolute paths break on other machines.

items.explanation: Correct: pinned versions let others recreate the setup.

items.stem: In pandas, which risk comes from chained indexing like df[df.a>0]['b'] = 1?

options.text: It may assign to a temporary copy and silently not change df
options.rationale: Correct: chained indexing can produce a SettingWithCopy problem.

options.text: It always raises an error and stops
options.rationale: It often warns rather than stopping, which is the danger.
It does not delete the column.

options.text: It converts df to a NumPy array
options.rationale: It does not change the DataFrame type.

items.explanation: Correct: chained indexing can produce a SettingWithCopy problem.
